title: Post-treatment risks of transcatheter aortic valve implantation: should we be increasing preventative measures?
authors: Panagiotis Theofilis; Panayotis K Vlachakis; George Koutsopoulos; Ioannis Kachrimanidis; Panagiotis Iliakis; Nikolaos Ktenopoulos; Polykarpos Christos Patsalis; Konstantinos Toutouzas; Konstantinos Tsioufis
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across an expanding risk spectrum. As indications extend to younger and lower-risk patients, post-treatment complications with implications for survival, quality of life, and valve durability require attention.
This narrative review discusses major post-TAVI complications with direct implications for procedural planning and lifetime management, including cerebrovascular events, conduction abnormalities, coronary obstruction and aortic root injury, bioprosthetic valve dysfunction, valve thrombosis, residual regurgitation, and TAVI-associated infective endocarditis. Evidence was reviewed from pivotal randomized trials, contemporary registries, consensus documents, systematic reviews, and mechanistic studies addressing incidence, pathophysiology, predictors, prognosis, prevention, diagnosis, and management of these complications.
Post-TAVI risk reduction should move beyond reactive complication management toward individualized prevention. Meticulous computed tomography-based planning, optimized valve selection and implantation technique, rational antithrombotic therapy, structured rhythm and valve surveillance, selective use of cerebral embolic protection, timely correction of clinically or hemodynamically significant residual regurgitation, and infection-prevention pathways are central components of contemporary care. Future progress will depend on better risk stratification, longer-term durability data, and targeted preventive strategies adapted to lower-risk patients with longer life expectancy.

title: Impact of the Extent, Pattern, and Location of Replacement Myocardial Fibrosis on Clinical Outcomes in Aortic Regurgitation.
authors: Bo Li; Linlin Dai; Yujie Liu; Zijuan Han; Yun Tang; Xingrui Chen; Aoxiang Zhang; Xuan Ma; Pengyu Zhou; Xi Jia; Wenqing Xu; Kaisaierjiang Aisikaier; Shengyao Han; Fen Sa; Kai Yang; Kankan Zhao; Chaowu Yan; Shihua Zhao; Xiuyu Chen
abstract:
The prognostic significance of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)-detected replacement myocardial fibrosis in aortic regurgitation (AR) remains incompletely understood. This study aims to explore the association between the extent, pattern, and location of LGE and clinical outcomes in patients with chronic AR.
Between 2010 and 2024, consecutive patients with moderate-to-severe AR and no significant coronary artery stenosis who underwent contrast-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) were included. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular mortality, heart transplantation, or rehospitalization for heart failure. The association between LGE characteristics and MACE was evaluated. Overall, 363 patients (mean age 52.6 ± 14.2 years; 54 female) were included. Over a median follow-up of 56.6 months, 73 patients experienced MACE. LGE was present in 200 patients (55.1%). An LGE extent threshold of 2.6% provided robust risk stratification, yielding the highest C-index of 0.797, a likelihood ratio chi-square of 97.30, and the lowest Akaike information criterion of 681.06. Furthermore, predominant subendocardial-involved LGE was present in 13.5% of LGE-positive patients and was independently associated with MACE after adjusting for LGE extent (HR 3.028; 95% CI 1.216-7.539; P = 0.017). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that patients with both LGE extent >2.6% and predominant subendocardial-involved LGE pattern were at the highest risk of MACE.
In AR, an LGE extent > 2.6% predicts MACE better than LGE presence alone. Furthermore, non-ischemic predominant subendocardial-involved LGE is independently associated with MACE. The coexistence of both features further amplifies the risk of MACE.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Anomalous Aortic Origin of Right Coronary Artery from the Left Coronary Sinus.
authors: Taeil Yang; Joonpyo Lee; Kil Yoon Pack; Kyung Eun Ha; Youngwoo Jang; Woong Chol Kang; Jeonggeun Moon
abstract:
Anomalous Aortic Origin of Right Coronary Artery (AAORCA) is a rare congenital anomaly that may be associated with adverse cardiac events, including sudden cardiac death. Surgical correction is commonly recommended in patients with AAORCA. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is a prevalent diagnostic modality, which increases AAORCA detection. However, the clinical significance of incidentally detected AAORCA remains unclear.
This non-randomized retrospective analysis included 10,134 patients who underwent CCTA between January 2014 and December 2022, either for suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) or a medical check-up. Three groups were created: patients with normal coronary anatomy (normal), with AAORCA (anomaly), and CAD without AAORCA (CAD). CAD was defined as a percentage diameter stenosis of ≥50% in one or more segments. Cardiac mortality was this study's primary endpoint.
Normal, anomaly, and CAD group comprised 7592 (74.9%), 66 (0.7%), and 2476 (24.4%) patients, respectively. During a median follow-up of 33.7 months (IQR: 13.2-53.4), Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed no significant difference in the cardiac death occurrence between the normal (15 events, 0.2%) and anomaly groups (0 events, 0%) (log-rank p=0.685). Cox proportional hazards model revealed no difference in mortality in the anomaly group compared with normal group.
In our cohort, incidentally detected AAORCA in adults did not demonstrate a clearly elevated cardiac death risk relative to CAD during mid-term follow-up. However, given the small number of events, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive rather than confirmatory evidence of a benign natural course, particularly in populations at higher risk of exertional sudden cardiac death.

title: Fibro-Inflammatory Signaling, Fibrosis, and Microvascular Ischemia as Convergent Translational Substrates of Sudden Cardiac Death in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Systematic Review.
authors: Antonio da Silva Menezes Junior; Isabela Jube Wastowski; Lilian Carla Carneiro
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) remains an important cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD), but the biological determinants of ventricular arrhythmic vulnerability remain incompletely defined. This systematic translational review examined whether fibro-inflammatory signaling, fibrotic remodeling, and microvascular ischemia represent convergent components of the arrhythmogenic substrate in HCM. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to January 2026. Of 167 records, 37 full-text reports were assessed and 11 studies included. Fibrosis emerged as the most clinically mature substrate marker, while microvascular ischemia appeared to amplify electrical instability, particularly in remodeled myocardium. Molecular and tissue studies suggested upstream fibro-inflammatory programs involving activated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix dysregulation, SMAD/TGF-beta signaling, CRLF1/LIFR-JAK-STAT signaling, and altered multicellular communication. Overall, the evidence supports an integrated mechanism-to-substrate model, but prospective outcome-validated studies are needed before these biological layers can refine SCD risk stratification beyond established clinical and imaging markers in contemporary HCM practice.

title: Conduction System Versus Right Ventricular Pacing in Patients Undergoing TAVR: A Multicenter Propensity-Matched Study.
authors: Felipe Diez-Delhoyo; Jorge Sanz-Sanchez; Guillem Muntane-Carol; Ignacio Jesus Amat-Santos; Juan Francisco Oteo Dominguez; Ricardo Rivera-Lopez; Lluis Asmarats; Manuel Pan; Jose Maria Novoa Medina; Juan Antonio Franco-Pelaez; Carlos Cuellas; Jessica Roa-Garrido; Maria Tamargo; Gabriela Veiga; Marta Herrero-Brocal; Pablo Miguel Valentin Garcia; Juan Garcia-Lara; Javier Cuesta; Felix Valencia-Serrano; Raquel Pimienta-Gonzalez; Jose Antonio Linares Vicente; Jorge Palazuelos-Molinero; Ivan Gomez-Blazquez; Josep Navarro-Manchon; Andrea Di Marco; Luis Garnacho-Gomez; Paula Vela-Martin; Cristina Martin-Arriscado; Fernando Sarnago Cebada
abstract:
Pacemaker implantation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is common and has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Cardiac physiological pacing (CPP) may preserve ventricular synchrony and reduce heart failure (HF) events compared with right ventricular pacing (RVP).
This study sought to compare long-term clinical outcomes of CPP vs RVP in patients requiring permanent pacing after TAVR.
Registro de Estimulación Fisiológica-TAVR is a retrospective, multicenter nationwide registry including patients undergoing TAVR and pacemaker implantation within 30 days. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using baseline clinical and echocardiographic variables, yielding 466 matched pairs. The primary endpoint was the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization. Cox proportional hazards models were used for time-to-event analyses. Median follow-up was 24 months.
In the propensity score-matched cohort, CPP was associated with a lower incidence of the primary endpoint than RVP (9.7% vs 17.6%; HR: 0.57; 95% CI: 0.39-0.83; P = 0.003). This difference was driven by fewer HF hospitalizations (7.9% vs 13.9%; HR: 0.57; 95% CI: 0.37-0.86; P = 0.008). No significant differences were observed in cardiovascular death or all-cause mortality between groups.
In this multicenter propensity score-matched study, CPP after TAVR was associated with a lower risk of the primary endpoint, driven by fewer HF hospitalizations. These findings support the need for further randomized clinical trials to evaluate the role of CPP in post-TAVR patients requiring ventricular pacing.

title: Impact of Extent of Coronary Artery Disease in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A PRO-TAVI Substudy.
authors: Gijs M Broeze; Hugo M Aarts; Johanna da Silva Voorham; Kimberley I Hemelrijk; Dirk Jan van Ginkel; Geert A A Versteeg; Maik J Grundeken; Bimmer E P M Claessen; Pim A L Tonino; Carl E Schotborgh; Martijn Meuwissen; Gert K van Houwelingen; Joanna J Wykrzykowska; Giovanni Amoroso; Tessel N Vossenberg; Pieter A Vriesendorp; Niels van Royen; Jurriën M Ten Berg; Jan G P Tijssen; Michiel Voskuil; Ronak Delewi; PRO-TAVI Investigators
abstract:
Coronary artery disease is present in one-half of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The recent randomized controlled PRO-TAVI (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation) trial indicated that deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is safe in patients with concomitant coronary artery disease at 1-year follow-up. The SYNTAX (Synergy between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with TAXUS and Cardiac Surgery) score quantifies the extent of coronary artery disease, which may guide individualized revascularization strategies.
The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between SYNTAX score (SS) and clinical outcomes in patients undergoing TAVR.
This study was a substudy of the PRO-TAVI trial, including 466 patients with significant coronary artery disease undergoing TAVR randomized to deferral of PCI or PCI before TAVR. SS was calculated from preprocedural coronary angiograms, and patients were stratified by SS quartiles. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and major bleeding at 1 year. An ischemic composite outcome of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and stroke was also assessed.
The primary composite outcome did not differ across SS categories between the deferral and PCI groups at 1-year follow-up, which was completed by all but 1 patient. In patients with SS >17, the ischemic composite outcome occurred more often in the deferral group (30.9% vs 14.8%; adjusted HR: 2.43; 95% CI: 1.04-5.64; P = 0.04), driven primarily by all-cause mortality and stroke. Bleeding events were less frequent in the deferral group across all SS subgroups.
In patients with concomitant coronary artery disease undergoing TAVR, deferral of PCI reduced bleeding risk and appeared safe across all SS categories. Deferral of PCI in patients with more complex coronary artery disease (SS >17) was associated with higher risk for the ischemic composite outcome. These post hoc findings require confirmation in randomized trials. (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation [PRO-TAVI]; NCT05078619).

title: Intraprocedural Cardiac Arrest in Patients Undergoing Percutaneous Coronary Interventions in the United States: An Analysis of the NCDR CathPCI Registry.
authors: Ramya C Mosarla; Binita Shah; Sunil V Rao; Sripal Bangalore; Pratik Manandhar; Leo Brothers; Jennifer Rymer; Nathaniel R Smilowitz
abstract:
Cardiac arrest (CA) during percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) is a catastrophic procedural complication. Contemporary rates of CA during PCI are unknown.
This study sought to understand contemporary rates of CA, associated mortality, and identify predictors of CA during PCI.
Patients with CA during PCI from 2018 to 2023 were identified from the National Cardiovascular Data Registry CathPCI Registry. Trends in intraprocedural CA (IPCA) incidence and in-hospital death were evaluated. Predictors of IPCA and risk-adjusted mortality were identified.
A total of 36,755 IPCA occurred during 3,956,840 PCIs (0.93%), including in 0.24% of elective PCIs, 0.32% of PCIs for stable coronary artery disease, and 1.28% of acute coronary syndrome interventions. The incidence of IPCA increased over time (0.62% in 2018 to 1.07% in 2023; P < 0.0001). In-hospital death occurred in 40.5% of patients with IPCA, 45.4% of whom died in the cardiac catheterization laboratory. Notably, although risk-adjusted IPCA increased (0.79% to 0.95%; P = 0.042), slight declines in risk-adjusted mortality (45.1% to 43.6%; P = 0.027) were observed over time. PCI for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, non-ST-segment acute coronary syndromes, increasing age, ventricular arrhythmias, severe aortic stenosis, vasopressors or inotrope use, mechanical circulatory support, coronary perforation, coronary dissection, cardiac tamponade, intraprocedural heart failure or myocardial infarction, and temporary cardiac pacemaker implantation were associated with increased adjusted odds of IPCA.
IPCA complicates 0.93% of contemporary PCI. Despite an increasing incidence of risk-adjusted IPCA, there were slight declines in risk-adjusted in-hospital mortality in the study period. Several patient and procedural characteristics were independently associated with intraprocedural CA.

title: Validating ECG-Based Artificial Intelligence Models for Cardiomyopathy Detection in Obstetric Patients: A Multisite International Study.
authors: Demilade Adedinsewo; Patrick W Johnson; Carolina Morales-Lara; Maria Vitoria Coutinho; Sabrina D Phillips; Marc A Eidelhoch; Michal Cohen-Shelly; Elad Maor; Ariel Furer; Abraham Tsur; Shali Mazaki-Tovi; Kamilu M Karaye; Bosede Bukola Afolabi; Olusoji Edward Jagun; Sadiq Hassan Ringim; Kehinde Femi Ibiyemi; Okechukwu Samuel Ogah; Sabha Bhatti; Shakeela Naz; Haleema Yasmin; Maedeh Ganji; Jose Ruiz; Khadeeja Esmail; Jason Wheatley; Anekwe Onwuanyi; Eric Chang; Myah M Griffin; Oludamilola Oluleye; Stefanie Gefroh; Mohan Krishna Ranganathan; Samir Awasthi; Yvonne Butler Tobah; Francisco Lopez-Jimenez; Zachi I Attia; Paul A Friedman; Peter A Noseworthy; Rickey E Carter
abstract:
Cardiomyopathy significantly impacts maternal health worldwide. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiograms (AI-ECG) have shown effectiveness in detecting left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) in adults and limited obstetric cohorts; however, broad validation in diverse obstetric populations remains unexplored.
Our primary objective was to validate the performance of 2 versions of an AI-ECG model for detecting cardiomyopathy in an international obstetric cohort.
We conducted a retrospective, multisite study of pregnant or postpartum women (≤12 months) across 11 institutions in 4 countries (Israel, Nigeria, Pakistan, and the United States). Two AI-ECG models (Food and Drug Administration-cleared v2.5.0 and refined v3.0.0) were evaluated against echocardiography. LVSD was defined as left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40% in keeping with the model's training target. Model performance was assessed by area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC).
We included 1,820 women with paired ECG-echocardiogram data, of whom 7.3% had LVSD. Model 1 (v2.5.0) demonstrated strong discriminative performance with an AUROC of 0.865, sensitivity of 46.1%, and negative predictive value of 95.8%. Model 2 (v3.0.0) showed significantly improved performance, with an AUROC of 0.925, sensitivity of 64.1%, and negative predictive value of 97.2% (P < 0.001) for LVSD detection.
AI-ECG models demonstrated strong external validity in a global obstetric cohort, with significantly improved performance in the refined model trained on expanded data. These findings support the potential role of AI-ECG for a scalable LVSD screening tool in obstetric populations, while underscoring the importance of population-specific validation prior to clinical implementation.

title: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis comparing Myval versus Sapien 3 transcatheter heart valves in severe aortic stenosis: focus on early and one-year mortality.
authors: Lin Yang; Guisong Yu; Mingchen Pan; Yandong Liu; Yuxi Zhu; Mengyu Zhang; Haigen Yu; Zhaohui Pei
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is a guideline-recommended treatment for severe aortic stenosis (AS). While the balloon-expandable Edwards Sapien 3 valve has long been the benchmark, the newer Myval valve has emerged as a potential alternative. Comparative data on mid-term survival, specifically one-year all-cause mortality, are lacking but crucial for clinical evaluation.
This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised direct comparative evidence on the Myval versus Sapien 3 valves in patients undergoing TAVI, searching PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central up to November 2025. The primary outcomes included all-cause mortality within 30 days and 1 year. Secondary outcomes were 30-day safety events and hemodynamic parameters.
Five studies (n = 2771) were included. The pooled analysis indicated no statistical difference in 30-day mortality (RR: 1.05, 95% CI: 0.53-2.07; p = 0.89; I2=0%) or in one-year all-cause mortality (RR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.64-1.35; p = 0.70; I2=0%). Rates of stroke, major bleeding, pacemaker implantation, and other 30-day complications were also comparable (all p > 0.05). Hemodynamically, the Myval valve was superior at 30 days, with a lower mean gradient (MD: -2.37, 95% CI: -3.45 to -1.30; p < 0.0001) and larger effective orifice area (MD: 0.26, 95% CI: 0.17-0.35; p < 0.00001). Available one-year data from two randomised trials indicated this hemodynamic benefit was sustained.
This updated meta-analysis demonstrates that the newer Myval valve offers comparable early safety and one-year survival to the established Sapien 3 valve, with superior and sustained hemodynamic performance. These findings support its role as a safe and effective alternative in the TAVI landscape.

title: Emergency Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation for Decompensated Aortic Stenosis accompanied by Cardiogenic Shock.
authors: Ajmer Singh; Christy P Kaliyadan; Praveen Chandra
abstract: Patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) often present acutely with decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic shock or cardiac arrest requiring immediate intervention. Treatment options for these patients include palliative care, balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV), emergency transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), or surgical aortic valve replacement. TAVI procedure is performed electively in majority of the patients. However, it can be considered a rescue therapy in patients with cardiogenic shock secondary to acutely decompensated valvular AS. Here, we report the successful use of emergent TAVI for a patient presenting with cardiogenic shock secondary to decompensated AS.

title: Adaptive Sealing in Protruding LVOT Calcification During TAVR: A 4-Patient Case Series.
authors: Ahmed M Salem; Karan Rao; Samuel Norman; Noman Ali; Michael S Cunnington; Daniel Blackman; Christopher J Malkin
abstract:
Protruding left ventricular outflow tract calcification represents a high-risk anatomical feature for transcatheter aortic valve replacement, predisposing to paravalvular regurgitation (PVR), annular injury, and conduction disturbance.
We present 4 patients with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis and protruding left ventricular outflow tract calcific nodules treated with the Navitor self-expanding valve system. Despite uniformly hostile landing-zone anatomy, procedural success was achieved in all cases. Residual PVR ranged from trivial to mild-to-moderate, with no patient developing moderate-or-greater PVR. All patients demonstrated hemodynamic improvement and early symptomatic benefit.
Calcific morphology and nodule orientation, rather than calcium burden alone, may be key determinants of PVR following Navitor implantation in hostile landing-zone anatomy. These findings are hypothesis-generating; the observed pattern of adaptive cuff sealing requires verification in larger, preferably comparative studies before conclusions regarding device-specific sealing mechanisms can be drawn.

title: [Sudden cardiac death and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy : risk assessment and indications for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator].
authors: Amaury Masson; Orianne de la Brassinne Bonardeaux; Nils de Marneffe; Vincenzo Miraglia; Caroline Piette; Patrizio Lancellotti
abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a myocardial disease characterized by left ventricular hypertrophy without abnormal loading conditions. Despite significant advances in management, HCM remains a major cause of sudden cardiac death, particularly in young individuals. Prevention relies on accurate arrhythmic risk stratification and the selective implantation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs). This article reviews current indications for primary prevention ICD implantation in sarcomeric HCM based on the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines and compares them with the more integrative approach proposed by the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA).

title: Temporal Trends in Hospitalization and Interventions for Aortic Stenosis in Canada, 2012-2024.
authors: Maria Servito; Denis Qeska; Suleman Aktaa; Philippe Pibarot; Jessica Forcillo; David Messika-Zeitoun; Janine Eckstein; Ellen Ross; Kendra MacFarlane; Seema Nagpal; Harindra C Wijeysundera
abstract:
Given the paradigm shift from surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) to transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), we examined the temporal trends in AS hospitalization and treatment across Canada.
Data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information Discharge Abstract Database were used for a population-based cross-sectional study of inpatients between April 1, 2012, and March 31, 2024. We estimated national and provincial rates and reported the annual changes in hospitalization for AS, SAVR, and TAVI. Rates were expressed as episodes/procedures per million, and stratified by age group, sex, and urban-vs-rural residence.
Between 2012 and 2024, hospitalizations for AS increased from 259.8 to 362.4 per million. Rates of SAVR declined from 104.4 to 66.5 per million, whereas rates of TAVI rose from 19.0 to 136.9 per million. The average annual per-million increases in AS hospitalizations were highest in Prince Edward Island (25.0), Nova Scotia (22.9), and Newfoundland and Labrador (21.3), particularly among individuals ≥ 80 years of age. The rates of SAVR declined, as the uptake of TAVI increased, with the shift mostly evident in those 60-79 years of age. Rates of TAVI were higher in men than in women, whereas AS hospitalizations were higher in rural than in urban areas.
Not unexpectedly there has been a dramatic shift from SAVR to TAVI observed, with an overall improvement in access to care. Nevertheless, sex-related and geographic disparities persist, highlighting the need for a coordinated national effort to ensure equitable access to AS management.

title: Acute Severe Aortic Regurgitation Immediately After Cardiopulmonary Bypass Initiation in a Patient With a Bicuspid Aortic Valve.
authors: Takumi Yamamoto; Keisuke Sumii
abstract: Antegrade cardioplegia delivery during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is standard practice in cardiac surgery, but it carries a risk of perfusion failure and acute myocardial distension in the presence of aortic regurgitation (AR). In patients with a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), acute exacerbation of AR can occur immediately after initiating CPB. An 80-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve (Sievers classification type 1: L/R fusion), severe aortic stenosis, mild AR, and an ascending aortic aneurysm underwent elective aortic valve replacement and ascending aortic replacement. Immediately after starting CPB and entering ventricular fibrillation (VF), the patient developed sudden, severe AR (vena contracta: 10 mm). This caused rapid left ventricular (LV) dilation and subsequent dislodgement of the LV vent cannula into the left atrium. Real-time transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) promptly identified both the severe AR and the cannula displacement. Following aortic cross-clamping, antegrade cardioplegia failed due to massive regurgitant volume overload into the LV. Prophylactically placed retrograde cardioplegia via the coronary sinus was immediately initiated, successfully achieving rapid cardiac arrest. The planned surgical procedures were completed successfully without further complications, and the patient was discharged in good condition on postoperative day 11. In this patient, the acute exacerbation of AR was likely driven by two key factors: first, a rapid elevation in the transvalvular pressure gradient following CPB onset and VF; and second, the unmasking of latent coaptation failure, stemming from BAV asymmetry and calcification, due to the loss of myocardial tone during VF. Real-time TEE monitoring and prophylactic placement of a retrograde cardioplegia cannula are critical for rapid diagnosis, troubleshooting, and ensuring effective myocardial protection.

title: Lipoprotein(a) Inhibition: Current Evidence, Therapeutic Landscape, and Future Directions.
authors: Pierre Sabouret; Domenico Mario Giamundo; Joanna Popiolek-Kalisz; Luigi Spadafora; Marco Bernardi; Elad Asher; Mamas A Mamas; Dan Atar; Giuseppe Andò
abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, apolipoprotein B-containing lipoprotein that contributes to cardiovascular risk through atherogenic, proinflammatory, and potentially antifibrinolytic mechanisms. Genetic, epidemiological, and mechanistic evidence supports a causal role for elevated Lp(a) in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve disease. In contrast, associations with other cardiovascular phenotypes are less consistent. Since circulating concentrations are largely inherited and only modestly affected by lifestyle measures and conventional lipid-lowering therapies, Lp(a) represents an important component of residual cardiovascular risk. This review summarizes the structural, genetic, and pathogenic characteristics of Lp(a), examines the strength of evidence across coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, calcific aortic valve disease, and heart failure, and discusses measurement, clinical interpretation, and potential biomarkers. The therapeutic landscape has expanded rapidly. Antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNA agents substantially suppress hepatic apolipoprotein(a) synthesis, oral small-molecule inhibitors prevent Lp(a) particle assembly, and in vivo gene-editing strategies aim to provide highly durable reductions. Early-phase trials have demonstrated marked lowering of circulating Lp(a); however, most were not designed to assess cardiovascular outcomes, so direct comparisons among agents are limited by differences in study populations, assays, dosing schedules, and follow-up. Ongoing cardiovascular outcome trials will determine whether selective Lp(a) lowering reduces clinical events and which patients are most likely to benefit. Until these results are available, Lp(a) measurement can refine risk stratification and support intensive management of modifiable risk factors, whereas biomarker reduction alone should not be equated with proven clinical benefit.

title: Lifetime management of valvular heart disease in younger and low risk patients.
authors: Laura Novelli; Nerea Fernández Ortiz; Guillem Murillo Varona; José Luis Diez Gil; Jorge Sanz Sanchez
abstract: Valvular heart disease in younger and low-risk patients presents unique therapeutic challenges because treatment decisions must account not only for immediate procedural success but also for the durability of the index intervention, the feasibility of future reinterventions, and the preservation of subsequent treatment options. Consequently, lifetime management has emerged as a longitudinal treatment paradigm in which every intervention influences the sequence, complexity, and outcomes of future procedures. Over the past decade, transcatheter valve therapies have expanded rapidly from a treatment reserved for elderly and high-surgical-risk patients to an increasingly adopted option in younger and lower-risk populations. Although contemporary evidence has demonstrated excellent procedural safety and mid-term outcomes, important uncertainties remain regarding long-term durability and the optimal management of structural valve deterioration and repeat interventions. These considerations highlight the importance of approaching each intervention not as an isolated procedure, but as a step within a predefined lifetime therapeutic strategy. In this context, structured Heart Team discussion and shared decision-making are fundamental to develop an individualized treatment plan that optimizes outcomes while preserving future surgical and transcatheter options across decades of patient care. This review aims to provide a practical framework for the lifetime management of aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valve disease in younger and low-risk patients.

title: Severe infections as collateral damage of decorative tattoos - A literature survey.
authors: Gevorg Aramian; Stefan Bereswill; Markus M Heimesaat
abstract: Tattooing is an ancient decorative cosmetic procedure with increasing popularity, but regulations concerning professional including hygienic practice are limited. Although mild inflammatory responses due to infections, for instance, are known complications, severe sequelae are beyond consideration. Here we summarize 40 cases of invasive and systemic infections as collateral damages of decorative tattooing. Reports from 14 countries revealed that most patients were male, with a median age of 28.5 years including a 6-week-old infant. Cases were categorized into deep abscesses and cellulitis, infective endocarditis, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, toxic shock syndrome, sepsis, and others. Overall, Gram-positive bacteria including Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci dominated as infectious agents. Thirty out of 40 patients were considered immunocompetent, 23 required surgical interventions alongside antimicrobial therapy, and five cases were fatal. Severe complications occurred due to soft-tissue destruction near the tattoo, hematogenous seeding to distant sites such as the heart valves, and toxin-mediated systemic responses; unregulated inadequate hygienic practices were risk factors for such collateral damages. In conclusion, severe tattoo-associated infections are rare events but can be fatal even in immunocompetent individuals. In cases of otherwise unexplained soft-tissue, systemic, or cardiac valve infections a tattooing history should be considered even if the tattoo site looks uninflamed.

title: Definition and Prognosis of Mitral Regurgitation in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: A Multicenter International Cohort Study.
authors: Laurenz Hauptmann; Christina Kronberger; Stéphanie K Schwarting; Daniela Tomasoni; Lara S Schlender; Sophia Koschatko; Maximilian Autherith; Charlotte Jantsch; Caglayan Demirel; Franz Duca; Andreas Kammerlander; Luca Bordignon; Gabriele Guidi Colombi; Nora Schwegel; Matteo Serenelli; Aldostefano Porcari; Steven A Muller; Nicolas Verheyen; Marish I F J Oerlemans; Maria Papathanasiou; Christian Hengstenberg; Marco Merlo; Jörg Hausleiter; Marianna Adamo; Philipp E Bartko; Christian Nitsche
abstract:
In transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, mitral regurgitation (MR) severity may be underestimated by conventional (semi-)quantitative echocardiographic criteria due to restrictive low-flow hemodynamics. We sought to define and validate disease-specific MR risk thresholds and compare their prognostic performance with guideline definitions.
In a multicenter cohort study (8 centers, 4 countries), 1101 patients with newly diagnosed transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (derivation, n=722; validation, n=379) underwent standardized echocardiography with blinded core laboratory analysis, including MR measures (vena contracta width, effective regurgitant orifice area, regurgitant volume, and regurgitant fraction). All-cause mortality and time to first heart failure hospitalization (HFH) served as end points. Prognostic thresholds were derived from spline analysis, validated externally, and compared with American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology, European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardiothoracic Surgery, and American Society of Echocardiography definitions.
During a median follow-up of 24.9 months (interquartile range, 12.0-42.0), 314 patients (28.5%) died and 244 (22.2%) experienced HFH. All MR metrics independently predicted mortality and HFH (all P<0.05). Spline-derived thresholds identified intermediate risk at vena contracta width ≥3.0 mm, effective regurgitant orifice area ≥0.10 cm2, regurgitant volume ≥15 mL, and regurgitant fraction ≥20% and high risk at effective regurgitant orifice area >0.25 cm2, regurgitant volume >38 mL, and regurgitant fraction >35%. Compared with guideline grading (≈12%-13%), the composite MR grading scheme classified a significantly higher proportion (21%) as severe MR and provided superior discrimination for clinical outcomes at 12 and 24 months in both the derivation and validation cohort. After multivariable adjustment, only the composite MR grading scheme remained strongly predictive for both mortality (hazard ratio, 1.20 [1.07-1.36]) and HFH (hazard ratio, 1.21 [1.05-1.38]).
Quantitative MR thresholds in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy are substantially lower than current guideline cutoffs. A validated, risk-based composite MR grading scheme improves prediction of both mortality and HFH, better reflecting the restrictive low-flow pathophysiology of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy and supporting disease-specific MR grading.

title: Advanced Rheumatic Heart Disease Complicated by Pregnancy, Mitral Valve Disease, Pulmonary Hypertension, and Left Atrial Thrombus: A Multidisciplinary Case Report from Resource-Limited Settings.
authors: Nouh Ismail Botan; Sadam Ismail Ahmed; Fatima Hachi Imaan; Kaltun Hassan Madar
abstract:
Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality among pregnant women in resource-limited settings. Pregnancy induces significant hemodynamic changes that can decompensate pre-existing valvular heart disease, leading to life-threatening complications for both mother and fetus.
A 27-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 6, para 5) at approximately 34-38 weeks presented with progressive shortness of breath, palpitations. Based on the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) classification, she was categorized as Class IV (extremely high risk) bilateral lower limb swelling, cough, fatigue, and reduced appetite. Cardiovascular examination revealed a systolic murmur, loud S1 and S2, with bilateral basal crepitations on respiratory examination. Echocardiography demonstrated an enlarged left atrium (5 cm), moderate mitral stenosis, mild mitral regurgitation, with fixed mitral valve leaflets, pulmonary hypertension, poor right ventricular function, a large left atrial thrombus, Labor occurred spontaneously while on low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). Mild pericardial effusion, and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (58%). Laboratory investigations showed elevated CRP (48.8 mg/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 99 ×109/L), mild coagulation abnormalities (INR 1.5), and urinalysis findings consistent with hematuria and proteinuria. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia, left atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy pattern, incomplete right bundle branch block, and prolonged QTc interval. The patient received multidisciplinary care including furosemide, metoprolol, and enoxaparin. She delivered a 2.1 kg neonate with good Apgar scores.
This case illustrates the severe maternal and fetal risks associated with advanced RHD during pregnancy. The presence of a large left atrial thrombus in a pregnant woman poses significant thromboembolic and hemodynamic risks. Multidisciplinary management involving cardiology, obstetrics, anesthesia, and intensive care is essential for optimizing outcomes.
This case highlights the critical importance of early recognition, strict adherence to CARE guidelines and multidisciplinary management, and the need for preventive strategies including primary prevention of rheumatic fever and secondary prophylaxis for RHD in resource-limited settings.

title: Heart failure in Somalia: a scoping review of the epidemiology, etiology, clinical characteristics, management, outcomes, and evidence gaps.
authors: Abdihamid Hirsi Abdulle; Khalid Hussein Ulusow; Abdullahi Abdi Yusuf; Abdisalam Ismail Hassan; Said Abdi Mohamed; Salma Mohamed Ahmed; Iqra Abdirazak Kabayare; Deka Ahmed Abdi; Aden Mohamed Hirsi; Ayan Mohamed Hassan
abstract:
Heart failure is an important cause of morbidity, hospitalisation, disability, and mortality, but evidence from Somalia remains fragmented and largely confined to individual hospital-based studies. This scoping review mapped the available evidence on the epidemiology, aetiologies, clinical and diagnostic characteristics, management, outcomes, and research gaps relating to heart failure in Somalia.
PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to 27 July 2026. Backward citation searching was conducted on 3 August 2026. Original studies reporting heart-failure-specific findings from Somalia, including Somaliland and Puntland, were eligible. Screening was conducted independently by two reviewers. Data were charted using a structured form and verified by a second reviewer. Findings were synthesised descriptively without meta-analysis because of substantial heterogeneity and possible participant overlap.
The searches identified 111 records, of which 56 were duplicates. Fifty-five records underwent title and abstract screening, 13 reports were assessed in full text, and 12 studies published between 2011 and 2025 were included. Eleven studies were associated with a single tertiary hospital in Mogadishu, and no study provided nationally representative or multicentre evidence. Reported aetiologies and associated conditions included hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, anaemia, thyroid dysfunction, renal disease, and thiamine-deficiency wet beriberi. Echocardiography was the principal diagnostic method, but heart-failure definitions and ejection-fraction thresholds varied substantially. Management data were limited mainly to selected populations with thyroid dysfunction, left ventricular thrombus, or wet beriberi. Outcome reporting was sparse and included in-hospital mortality, first-year outcomes in a thrombus cohort, length of stay, stroke, thrombus resolution, and exploratory prognostic indices.
The evidence on heart failure in Somalia is emerging but remains geographically concentrated, methodologically heterogeneous, and insufficient to estimate national burden, treatment coverage, or long-term outcomes. Prospective multicentre studies and a staged heart-failure registry using standardised diagnostic definitions, clear denominators, treatment indicators, and longitudinal follow-up are needed.

title: Automatic transesophageal echocardiographic evaluation of patients with mitral valve prolapse: comparison with patients without structural cardiac chamber remodeling (an exploratory study).
authors: Marcelo Luiz Campos Vieira; Ana C T Rodrigues; Edgar Daminello; Adriana Reche; Gustavo P de Almeida; Alessandra J Oliveira; Luiz O A Santos; Rafael B Piveta; Rodrigo A C Meirelles; Cláudia G Monaco; Fernando C Oliveira; Fernando A Solis; Wercules Oliveira; Alessandro C Lianza; Adriana Sanudo; Edgar B Lira Filho; Sérgio A F Curcio; Robinson Poffo; Cláudio H Fischer; Samira S Morhy
abstract:
There is a paucity of information concerning automatic mitral valve apparatus (MVA) analysis of patients with mitral valve prolapse (MVP). We aimed to study with an automatic three-dimensional (3D) transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)-dedicated software, patients with moderate and severe mitral regurgitation when compared to patients with no structural cardiac chamber alterations [patients with patent foramen ovale (PFO) who underwent TEE].
We employed TEE software dedicated to automatic analysis of 34 parameters of the MVA, comparing MVP patients with moderate and severe mitral regurgitation and patients with PFO without cardiac chamber structural alterations. Mitral valve effective regurgitant orifice (ERO) and regurgitant volume were correlated to automatic MVP parameters.
Fifty-nine MVP patients and 43 PFO patients were analyzed. All MVP patients presented P2 MVP, 15 (25.4%) with both posterior and anterior prolapse. Twenty-seven automatic parameters (79%) were different concerning MVP and PFO patients (P<0.05): diameters, area, perimeter, height, angle, coaptation width, length, closure line length, and annulus. ERO was 0.43±0.11 cm2, and regurgitant volume was 62.9±14.9 mL/beat. Automatic analysis correlated to 75th percentile ERO MVP patients (ERO >0.48 cm2): posterior leaflet area (r=0.74, P=0.03); posterior leaflet length (r=0.73, P=0.03); tenting area (r=0.41, P=0.048).
Automatic mitral valve parameters differed significantly between patients with MVP and those without structural cardiac chamber remodeling. In exploratory analysis, patients in the upper range of ERO values (≥75th percentile) showed patterns involving posterior leaflet geometry that were consistent with the associations observed in continuous-variable analysis. These findings support the potential role of automated 3D assessment in the anatomical characterization of MVP.

title: Outcomes and Predictors of Inpatient Mortality for Infective Endocarditis in Patients with Malignancy: Contemporary Nationwide Study from the United States.
authors: Krishna Sanaka; Bo Xu
abstract: Infective endocarditis (IE) in patients with malignancy represents a high-risk clinical cohort, yet nationwide data on outcomes and predictors of mortality remain limited. Using the United States National Inpatient Sample (2016-2022), we identified hospitalizations involving IE and a malignancy diagnosis. Inpatient mortality, complications, and temporal trends were analyzed overall and across malignancy subtypes, causative organisms, and prosthetic valve status. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was performed across the full IE cohort. Of 635 715 IE hospitalizations, 44 060 (6.9%) involved a malignancy diagnosis. Inpatient mortality was higher in this group than among IE hospitalizations without malignancy (13.5% vs 9.8%; P < .001), and malignancy remained associated with mortality after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.19-1.39; P < .001). The proportion of IE hospitalizations involving malignancy increased from 6.7% in 2016 to 7.7% in 2022. Fungal infection, shock, acute kidney injury, and stroke were associated with mortality. Prosthetic-valve IE had lower mortality than non-prosthetic-valve IE (7.7% vs 13.9%; P < .001). These findings identify a high-risk, heterogeneous phenotype and support earlier diagnostic evaluation and coordinated oncology, cardiology, and infectious diseases management.

title: Bentall Procedure in a Patient with Loeys-Dietz Syndrome: A Case Report.
authors: Dheeraj Arora; Supriya Chaudhary; Rajesh Madavathazathil Gopalakrishnan; Sameer Bhate
abstract: Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS) is a rare autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder characterized by aggressive aortopathy, craniofacial anomalies and systemic involvement. Rapid aortic root dilatation and valvular dysfunction mandate an early surgical intervention. We report a case of 15-year-old boy with LDS, rapidly progressive aortic root dilatation and severe aortic regurgitation (AR) who underwent successful Bentall procedure. The case highlights the need of early detection, multidisciplinary involvement and meticulous anesthetic care.

title: Time for Change: Strengthening Early Detection and Intervention Strategies to Improve Cardiovascular Health in Canada.
authors: Andriy Katyukha; Kendra Pelland; Santabhanu Chakrabarti; David Messika-Zeitoun; Stephanie Poon; Anne Simard; Harindra C Wijeysundera; Seema Nagpal
abstract: Cardiovascular disease remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada, and early detection and intervention programs have the potential to improve outcomes for patients. This review aims to outline the importance of early detection and intervention for various cardiac diseases, outline barriers that exist to early detection in Canada, identify the system-level benefits to improving early detection and intervention, and ultimately help policymakers and other stakeholders identify new opportunities for intervention. Various data show that early detection and intervention in coronary artery disease, arrhythmias, valvular heart disease, and heart failure are feasible and are associated with better outcomes for patients. Recognizing the unique barriers that exist in Canada, we must work toward creating innovative solutions aimed at helping patients access care. Several innovative collaborative models of care and programs have been piloted around the world, allowing us to learn from different jurisdictions and begin work locally to help improve early detection of cardiovascular diseases in Canada. Canadian stakeholders including health leaders, policymakers, and other health advocates must continue to work with physician leaders to create robust, comprehensive, and cost-effective early detection and intervention programs to improve cardiac care nationally.

title: Meta-analysis of the histopathological features of surgically removed aortas classified according to the SCVP and AECVP consensus documents.
authors: Eemeli Jämsen; David Kalfeřt; Tero Halmesmäki; Ari Mennander; Timo Paavonen; Ivana Kholová
journal: American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
abstract: The Society for Cardiovascular Pathology (SCVP) and the Association for European Cardiovascular Pathology (AECVP) published consensus statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta to unify nomenclature and provide a new classification scheme to systematically evaluate the degenerative and inflammatory lesions of the thoracic aorta. The aim of this meta-analysis was to determine the histopathological features of thoracic aneurysmatic aortas, thoracic dissected aortas, and thoracic aortas in patients with a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). Additionally, the aim was to map how consensus documents and classification schemes is used in practice and research. Articles for analysis were identified while searching for references to the SCVP and AECVP consensus documents, resulting in 174 articles. After applying the exclusion and inclusion criteria, 10 articles were included in the analysis. Four cohorts were analysed: the whole cohort, the aneurysm cohort, the dissection cohort, and the BAV cohort. Medial degeneration was found in all cohorts. The dissection cohort showed more severe medial degeneration than the aneurysm cohort or the BAV cohort. The BAV cohort showed the mildest medial degeneration compared to the other cohorts. More prevalent smooth muscle cell nuclei loss was linked to dissection. The BAV cohort showed milder changes in elastic fibers. Atherosclerosis was comparable among all cohorts. Medial degeneration represents the pathological process of several aortic diseases. All studied components of medial degeneration were present in aneurysms, dissections, and BAV aortas. The consensus documents have been useful tools and assist with the systematic evaluation of resected aortas, although their use in the complexity is limited.

title: Improved Visualization of Heart Valves With 4D-CT Using a Novel Motion Correction Algorithm.
authors: Daniel Zedler; Tristan T Demmert; André Ritter; Thomas Allmendinger; Bernhard Schmidt; Albert M Kasel; Omer Dzemali; Robert Manka; Victor Mergen; Thomas Flohr; Matthias Eberhard; Hatem Alkadhi
abstract:
Motion artifacts remain a limitation of cardiac CT when assessing both native and prosthetic heart valves, particularly during phases of rapid motion. This may lead to reduced image quality, potentially impairing the evaluation of valvular movement and pathology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether a novel reconstruction-based motion correction algorithm improves image quality and reduces motion artifacts of native and prosthetic heart valves compared with standard reconstructions in photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT).
In this retrospective single-center study, 57 patients [21 women; median age, 71 (interquartile range, 57 to 78 y)] who underwent clinically indicated 4D cardiac CT for suspected native and prosthetic valvular disease were included. Images were acquired using retrospectively electrocardiography (ECG)-gated spiral dual-source PCD-CT without ECG-pulsing. Images were reconstructed in 10% steps throughout the RR-interval using both standard (TrueStack) and an otherwise identical reconstruction using the novel motion correction algorithm (ZeeFreePlus). Subjective image quality and motion artifacts were independently assessed by 2 blinded, experienced readers using a 4-point visual analog scale for 3 categories: valve frame/annulus, valve leaflets, and valvular pathology. Objective analysis included quantification of the volume of artifacts throughout the cardiac cycle.
A total of 68 valves were evaluated, including 57 prosthetic valves (22 transcatheter aortic valve replacements and 19 surgical valves, 11 mitral valves, and 5 tricuspid valve interventions) and 11 native valves. Valvular pathology was present in 29 cases, with the most prevalent being hypoattenuated leaflet thickening in 14/29 (48%). Motion-corrected reconstructions significantly improved image quality and reduced motion artifacts across all cardiac phases and all categories (all, P<0.001). The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole (P<0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology (P<0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm (P<0.001).
A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

title: Temporary Left Ventricular Unloading With Impella as a Bridge to Emergency Surgery for Acute Mitral Bioprosthetic Failure.
authors: Osamu Kinoshita; Takuma Aoki; Satoru Murata; Kento Murohara; Wataru Iai
abstract: Structural valve deterioration usually declares itself gradually, but a bioprosthetic leaflet that tears away from a stent post can produce catastrophic regurgitation without warning. In the mitral position, the left atrium has not had time to become compliant, and the resulting rise in pulmonary capillary pressure can flood the lungs within hours. A 68-year-old woman who had undergone mitral valve replacement with a bovine pericardial bioprosthesis 13 years earlier developed sudden dyspnea. Her oxygen saturation was 58%, the chest radiograph showed almost complete bilateral opacification, and the pH was 7.042 with a lactate of 8.8 mmol/L. She was intubated after noninvasive ventilation failed. Catheterization excluded coronary disease and showed a cardiac index of 1.32 L/minute/m², a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 35 mmHg, and a wedge pressure of 22 mmHg. Echocardiography demonstrated severe regurgitation through the prosthesis with an abnormally mobile leaflet. Emergency surgery was indicated, but the operating room was occupied, and a wait of several hours was expected. With the pulmonary artery pressure rising, an Impella CP (Abiomed, Danvers, MA) was implanted approximately 11 hours after arrival and supported the circulation for five hours until cardiopulmonary bypass was established. During that interval, the rise in pulmonary artery pressure did not continue; the cardiac index and mixed venous oxygen saturation increased, and oxygenation was maintained despite a reduction in the fraction of inspired oxygen. Mean pulmonary artery pressure nevertheless remained approximately 40 mmHg. One leaflet was found torn away from a stent post and prolapsing into the left atrium; the valve was replaced with a porcine bioprosthesis. Postoperatively, she required hemodiafiltration for acute kidney injury and temporary pacing for bradyarrhythmia; the course was further complicated by small cerebral infarcts and a right phrenic nerve palsy. She was extubated on day 10 and discharged home on day 48, remaining in New York Heart Association class I at review on day 108. When definitive surgery for acute left-sided valvular failure must be delayed for logistical reasons, temporary left ventricular unloading may be considered as a means of protecting the lung during the wait. In this patient, it was associated with maintained oxygenation and improved systemic hemodynamics, although its independent contribution cannot be determined from a single case.

title: Understanding pedagogical challenges faced by technology teachers in special needs classrooms
authors: Katane Elizabeth Kekana; Thokozani Isaac Mtshali
journal: Journal of Education and Learning Technology
abstract: Teaching learners with special educational needs requires dynamic and adaptive pedagogical strategies that can lead to social development and academic success. This can be possible if teachers are assisted in mitigating the daily challenges of teaching such learners. This qualitative exploratory case study investigated the pedagogical challenges encountered by two Grade 9 Technology teachers in the Capricorn District of Limpopo Province. This study used Shulman’s Content and Pedagogical Knowledge framework to understand teachers’ challenges. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations; all collected data were analysed thematically. This study found that teachers experienced various challenges, including the emotional labour of teaching, burnout in the LSEN environment and the enactment of instructional knowledge. The study concluded that the sampled teachers displayed weaknesses in lesson planning, activating learners’ prior knowledge, diagnosing errors, achieving curriculum objectives and sustaining engagement. As a result, it was recommended that support through teacher assistants, creative differentiated strategies and enhanced digital-technology literacy to improve outcomes for learners with special needs was imminent.

title: Integration of Biomechanics and Digital Technology: Using Kinovea for Motion Analysis and Learning for Beginner Athletes
authors: Muhammad Nur Hudha; Riezky Maya Probosari; Annisa Nur Khasanah; Supurwoko; Salsabila Kholifahtun Nisa’; Gifran Rihla Gifarka Latief
journal: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science
abstract: Background: The integration of biomechanics with digital motion-analysis technologies has introduced new approaches for examining movement efficiency, kinematic characteristics, and technical patterns in walking and running activities. Kinovea, as an accessible motion-analysis software, provides both visual and quantitative feedback. However, its application in supporting technique development among beginner athletes remains insufficiently explored. Aim: This study aims to describe the use of Kinovea in biomechanics training and examine its contribution to the awareness of kinematic characteristics and movement techniques among beginner athletes. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design involved 72 beginner athletes aged 18–25 years selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected over 16 weeks through interviews, field observations, and motion video recordings analyzed using Kinovea. Kinematic data focused on joint angles, stride behavior, and movement phases during walking, running, and the flight phase. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo 12, while kinematic results were interpreted descriptively to identify performance patterns and areas for technical refinement. Result: Kinematic analysis showed coordinated joint-angle patterns across all phases. Walking analysis identified arm swing angles of 50.9°–58.8° and leg separation angles of 64.3°–67.2°, indicating a stable gait rhythm. The running analysis revealed knee angles of 68.8°–69.8° and elbow angles of 87.6°–89.1°, indicating efficient propulsive mechanics. The flight phase demonstrated knee angles of 81.2°–87.8° and elbow angles of 80.4°–88.3°, suggesting effective momentum use and postural stability. These measurements supported stride-efficiency assessment and technique evaluation. Qualitative findings revealed that Kinovea enabled athletes to interpret movement phases and identify technical inefficiencies through slow-motion and frame-by-frame visualization. Conclusion: Kinovea supports basic motion analysis by providing clear kinematic information and helping beginner athletes observe and refine their movement techniques. The findings also offer practical value for coaches by enabling more precise identification of inefficient patterns and guiding targeted corrections during early-stage training.

journal: Научный журнал "Вестник Актюбинского регионального университета имени К. Жубанова"
abstract: In the context of increasing complexity of modern network infrastructures and the growing number of cyberattacks, improving the effectiveness of intrusion detection systems is a highly relevant task. The aim of this work is to develop and investigate a hybrid approach to network attack detection based on a combination of signature-based analysis and intelligent machine learning methods.  The research methods include analysis of requirements for anomaly detection systems, comparative analysis of existing solutions, design of a hybrid system architecture, and experimental modeling using multiclass classification of network traffic. The results demonstrate that integrating a neural model with a traditional detection system improves attack detection coverage and reduces the number of false positives.  The practical significance of the study lies in the possibility of deploying the proposed architecture in real corporate networks, while the theoretical significance consists in substantiating the effectiveness of a hybrid approach to traffic analysis. Future research directions include adaptive model training and expansion of the range of detectable attacks.
